blocks.text: A mature iroko tree lifts hundreds of litres of water more than thirty metres into the air every day, with no pump and no moving parts. Cut a stalk of Talinum and stand it in red ink, and within an hour thin red lines appear in the stem. Those lines are the pipes.

blocks.markdown:
## Two sets of pipes

Flowering plants have two transport tissues, and together they make up the vascular bundle.

**Xylem** carries water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots upward to the leaves. Movement is in one direction only. The vessels are long tubes made of dead, hollow cells whose end walls have broken down, and their walls are strengthened with **lignin**, which also helps support the plant.

**Phloem** carries dissolved food, mainly sucrose and amino acids, from the leaves to wherever it is needed — growing buds, developing fruits, storage roots. This movement is called **translocation** and it can go up or down. Phloem sieve tubes are made of living cells with perforated end walls, and each is accompanied by a companion cell that supplies the energy, because translocation is an active process.

blocks.title: Transpiration
blocks.text: The loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. It is an unavoidable consequence of having stomata open for carbon dioxide, but the plant turns it to advantage by using it to pull water up the xylem.

blocks.markdown:
### The path of water from soil to air

Follow a single water molecule.

1. Soil water is more dilute than the sap of a **root hair cell**, so it enters by **osmosis** across the partially permeable membrane. The root hair is long and thin, giving a very large surface area.
2. Water passes from cell to cell across the root cortex, again by osmosis, moving down a gradient of water potential.
3. It enters the **xylem vessels** of the root.
4. It is drawn up the xylem as a continuous column, held together by the cohesion between water molecules and their adhesion to the vessel walls.
5. In the leaf it moves into the mesophyll cells and evaporates into the air spaces.
6. The vapour diffuses out through a **stoma** into the atmosphere.

The evaporation at step 5 is what creates the **transpiration pull**. Removing water from the top of the column puts the whole column under tension, so more water is pulled up from below. Root pressure and capillarity contribute, but transpiration pull is the main force, and it costs the plant no energy.

### Factors affecting the rate of transpiration

Anything that speeds up evaporation or steepens the water vapour gradient increases transpiration.

- **Light intensity** — bright light opens the stomata, so transpiration rises. In darkness stomata close and transpiration falls to a minimum.
- **Temperature** — higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy, so evaporation and diffusion are faster.
- **Humidity** — high humidity means the air outside already holds much vapour, so the diffusion gradient is shallow and transpiration slows.
- **Wind** — moving air sweeps away the layer of saturated air at the leaf surface, keeping the gradient steep, so transpiration rises.
- **Available soil water** — if the soil is dry the plant closes its stomata to conserve water and transpiration falls sharply.
- **Surface area and number of stomata** — a plant with many large leaves transpires faster than a cactus with spines.

blocks.title: Interpreting a wilting experiment
blocks.prompt: Two identical leafy shoots are placed in tubes of water. Shoot A is left as it is; shoot B has petroleum jelly smeared over the lower surface of every leaf. After three hours, shoot A has taken up 4 cm³ of water and shoot B only 1 cm³. Explain the results.

steps.text: Identify what petroleum jelly does. It is waterproof and airtight, so it blocks the stomata it covers.
Recall where the stomata are. In most dicotyledonous leaves the great majority of stomata are on the lower surface, which reduces water loss by keeping them out of direct sun.
Link water uptake to water loss. A shoot takes up water to replace what it transpires, so uptake is a fair measure of transpiration.

Explain shoot B. With the lower surface sealed, most stomata are blocked, so water vapour can escape only through the few upper stomata and slowly through the cuticle. Transpiration, and therefore uptake, drops to about a quarter.
Draw the conclusion. The comparison shows both that most transpiration occurs through the stomata and that most stomata are on the lower leaf surface.

blocks.answer: Shoot B lost far less water because the petroleum jelly blocked the stomata on the lower surface, where most stomata are found. This shows that transpiration takes place mainly through the stomata of the lower surface.

blocks.title: Ringing experiment
blocks.text: If a complete ring of bark, which contains the phloem, is removed from a tree trunk, the region above the ring swells with accumulated sugar while the roots below eventually starve and the tree dies. This is the classic proof that phloem, and not xylem, carries manufactured food downwards.

blocks.title: Wording that scores
blocks.text: Say water is 'pulled' up the xylem by transpiration pull, not 'pushed' or 'sucked'. And remember that mineral salts enter root hairs by active transport while water enters by osmosis — questions often test the two in the same sentence.

points: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards in dead, lignified vessels; phloem translocates sucrose and amino acids in living sieve tubes.
Water enters root hairs by osmosis and mineral salts enter by active transport.
Transpiration pull, created by evaporation from the leaves, is the main force lifting water up the xylem.
Transpiration is increased by light, heat and wind, and decreased by high humidity and dry soil.
Ringing a tree removes the phloem and shows that food is translocated downwards through it.
